content: Presenilins-associated rhomboid-like protein (PARL) is a mitochondrial inner membrane protein encoded by the PARL gene located on chromosome 3 in humans. It belongs to the rhomboid family of intramembrane serine proteases. This protein plays a critical role in signal transduction, programmed cell death (apoptosis), neurodegenerative diseases, and type 2 diabetes. Structure Proteins in the rhomboid family share a conserved structural core consisting of six transmembrane helices (TMHs). The catalytic dyad, which is essential for enzymatic activity, is formed by serine and histidine residues located within TMH-4 and TMH-6, respectively. This catalytic dyad is situated deep within the hydrophobic environment of the phospholipid bilayer, indicating that peptide bond hydrolysis occurs within the membrane itself. As a member of the Parl subfamily, PARL contains an additional N-terminal transmembrane helix, which may form a loop structure that connects to the catalytic core. Function The PARL gene encodes an integral mitochondrial membrane protein. After proteolytic processing, this protein generates a small peptide known as P-beta, which is subsequently transported to the nucleus. PARL is implicated in signal transduction through a process called regulated intramembrane proteolysis, which involves the cleavage of membrane-anchored precursor proteins. Variations in the PARL gene have been linked to an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Furthermore, alternative splicing of this gene results in multiple transcript variants that encode different isoforms. PARL also plays a significant role in apoptosis. It interacts with the mitochondrial GTPase optic atrophy 1 (OPA1) and the Bcl-2 family-related protein HAX1. OPA1 primarily regulates mitochondrial fusion within the inner mitochondrial membrane. However, after being cleaved by PARL, the shorter, soluble form of OPA1 helps inhibit apoptosis by reducing the release of cytochrome c, thereby suppressing pro-apoptotic signaling. Alternatively, PARL can prevent apoptosis by working with HAX1 to activate the HtrA2 protease, which prevents the accumulation of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax. Clinical Significance A specific mutation in PARL, known as p.S77N, has been studied and found not to be a common cause of early-onset Parkinson’s disease. However, variations in the sequence or expression of PARL (also referred to as PSARL) may represent a novel risk factor for type 2 diabetes and other components of metabolic syndrome. Additionally, mutations in the PARL gene have been implicated in Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, a condition characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction that leads to the death of retinal ganglion cells and subsequent neurodegeneration. Interactions PARL has been shown to interact with several key proteins, including: PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1), OPA1 (optic atrophy 1), and HAX1 (HCLS1-associated protein X-1).
